newsitem.title: JAPAN: Record low turnout shows Japan democracy ailing.
newsitem.headline: Record low turnout shows Japan democracy ailing.

text.p: Democracy looked like being a loser in Japan's general election on Sunday.
Voters stayed away from the ballot box in droves and little over half the electorate bothered to exercise their democratic right to choose their representatives in parliament.
Commentators said the record low turnout of 59 percent suggests that politics is becoming an irrelevance for a growing number, boding ill for the health of Japanese democracy.

"While many people around the world have spilled blood to win democracy, it was given to us in Japan," said Junichiro Koizumi, an outspoken senior legislator belonging to the Liberal Democratic Party. "The figure means that close to half of Japan said 'Do as you please'."
The eight percentage point fall in turnout from the last general election in July 1993 translates to 10 million newly disaffected potential voters.

After Japan's defeat in World War Two, the U.S. military occupation reduced the monarchy to a symbolic role and introduced democratic reforms. But many believe a vibrant parliamentary democracy never fully took root, leaving real control in the hands of bureaucrats and big business.

Political analysts and legislators blamed three main factors for the no-shows this time -- a lack of clear issues, a new electoral system which confused voters, and distaste for politics after a period of revolving-door governments.
"For the record low voter turnout, the biggest blame should go to the politicians," said Yomiuri Shimbun commentator Hidekazu Miyama.
"It can be said that the citizens turned their backs on the degraded state of politics, with its last-minute flattery aimed at voters and its never-ending squabbles ignoring basic principles."
The 1993 election broke the mould of Japanese politics by depriving the Liberal Democratic Party of the majority it had enjoyed since 1955.
But hopes of a new age of reformist politics, in contrast with the scandal-ridden but stable rule of the LDP, withered in the confusion of coalition politics.
Japan has seen three prime ministers come and go since 1993.
In April 1994, popular anti-graft campaigner Morihiro Hosokawa resigned as premier after pressure from the then opposition LDP over a loan affair.
Hosokawa's successor Tsutomu Hata lasted only two months, because the Socialists, the biggest party in the anti-LDP coalition government, walked away from the alliance.

In June 1994, the LDP staged a surprise comeback by offering a huge compromise to form an unthinkable alliance with the leftist Socialist Party -- handing the post of prime minister to its leader Tomiichi Murayama.
Last January Murayama, weary at coalition infighting, stepped down and handed over the government to the LDP's Ryutaro Hashimoto.
Graft, the key issue in the 1993 elections, gave birth to a new electoral system which combined single-seat constituencies with proportional representation.
But a lack of a thorough public awareness campaign meant that some voters did not even know where they belonged in the 300 new constituencies that replaced the 129 old multi-seat districts.

In addition, the politicians who drafted the political reform bills introduced a safety net for themselves, allowing candidates in single-seat districts to also compete on the proportional representation list.

"The politicians thought only of saving their own necks when they passed those political reform bills in 1994," said political analyst Yoichi Masuzoe. "The self-serving nature of those reforms backfired in the form of low turnout."
